title: At Apollo Hospitals, clinicians use a continuous learning AI system to improve patient safety reviews
summary: Apollo Hospitals clinicians and Microsoft FDEs built an AI system to help improve patient safety review process
body_markdown:
It’s 1 p.m. on a Wednesday afternoon in Chennai and Dr. Rohini Sridhar is leading the daily review of adverse events occurring at Apollo Hospitals’ network across India. As chief of medical services, she and her colleagues on the clinical governance team analyze incidents relating to patient care—be it a fall, medication error or readmission—to determine why they happened and whether procedures need to be changed to prevent similar cases.


Assisting them in this important task of guarding patient safety is the Daily Tiered Huddle (DTH) agent, an AI solution developed with[Microsoft Frontier Company](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company) ’s forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) using[Microsoft Foundry](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/ai-foundry/) . The agent reads hospital data collected in[Microsoft Fabric](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-fabric) and flags patient-care incidents requiring review based on set parameters. It then summarizes these incidents, prompts clinicians for further information and suggests case assessments using[Microsoft Work IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en/copilot/features/work-iq) —Microsoft’s intelligence layer for bringing organizational data, context and AI reasoning together.


For example, if a patient returned to the intensive care unit within 48 hours, Dr. Sridhar can read such details as a timeline of their treatment, which medication was administered and blood test results, just by clicking on the patient’s ID in the DTH agent. And if she thinks facts like low magnesium levels or a urinary tract infection are relevant to the incident, she can discuss it with the doctor who’s briefing at their daily huddle.


A year ago, she would have asked clinicians for these details to get a fuller picture of what happened, then waited hours or days while the answers were gathered manually from various records in the hospital. With about 600 such adverse events reported monthly across Apollo’s 55 main hospitals, those delays meant an incident review could take days.


“For anyone to process 600 cases per month with incomplete data and come up with a meaningful decision is difficult,” says Dr. Sridhar, a trained pathologist. “Now, we have the data that’s required for us to make an analysis.”


After a case is reviewed, it can be flagged for further discussion using tags like COQR (clinical outcomes and quality review) and RCA (root cause analysis). Photo by Selvaprakash Lakshmanan for Microsoft.


At today’s huddle, several cases can be closed with no further action needed. A handful are flagged for further checks and discussion using tags in the agent like COQR (clinical outcomes and quality review) and RCA (root cause analysis). There are no sentinel events, which refer to a serious patient safety incident resulting in death or severe harm.


Since the DTH agent was rolled out, Apollo’s records show over 60% of cases reviewed by the huddle are closed within three days.* This means the clinical governance team can turn their attention to the more-complex cases that may impact safety policies and protocols.


“We are able to decide that only the 40% are actually relevant for us to do a deeper dive,” says Dr. Sridhar. “Now we are able to intervene early, propose solutions and proceed toward prevention, which is a huge advantage.”


### **Building a customized AI solution with FDEs**


Having such a customized AI solution at their disposal, Dr. Sridhar says, was largely due to Microsoft Frontier Company’s FDEs, who “were deeply immersed” in the doctors’ daily processes.


“The FDEs made that process much easier for us,” she says. “This ability to listen to the idea, then devise a tool to draw in the data from wherever it is sitting on Fabric, bring it all together in a manner that works for the user. They’ve done it much faster than I thought would be possible.”


Being there throughout, from initial calls with the clinical governance team to having the DTH agent in production at some hospitals, was crucial, says James Edwards, one of the four FDEs who worked on this project.


“What I really enjoy about being an FDE is doing discovery with the customer—trying to understand what problems they’re facing and where’s the right place for us to build an agent that can help them,” he says. “We bring the technical expertise on what’s actually possible, which is especially important as we’re trying to do things at the cutting edge with AI.”


By participating in the clinicians’ workflows directly, the FDE team could identify their implicit knowledge, translate it into the agent’s capabilities, and continuously refine the system based on clinical feedback.


On top of daily calls with clinicians and observing the huddles, Microsoft engineers worked closely with Apollo’s tech team to match the electronic health-records data already being collected by the hospital against data that was important for the governance team, to automate how the agent processes it. During the development process, engineers used synthetic data for their evaluations and testing, and not Apollo’s electronic health records.


Apollo’s chief information officer, Ashokkan Somuveerappan, says the FDEs performed better than traditional software engineers because they prioritized the outcome instead of only completing their individual tasks.


Apollo Hospitals’ chief information officer Ashokkan Somuveerappan . Photo by Selvaprakash Lakshmanan for Microsoft.


“They were more glued to the outcome that they needed to achieve,” he says. “They would step in to get a job done. It’s a different, innovative way of working—traditionally you have separate engineers for the app, the database, the UI. Now a single person can work across the different areas.”


### **A continuous learning loop and trend-spotter**


The DTH agent isn’t just a productivity tool to make reviews run more smoothly. It is also a continuous learning system that ingests what the medical experts discuss at the daily huddles, using[Microsoft Work IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en/copilot/features/work-iq) for context.


“The agent is reading all of this data from Fabric and actually writing things back into Fabric as well,” says Edwards. “So, it becomes not just the source of data for the patient histories, but also for these cases themselves—the types of decisions that are made and the types of questions that are being asked.”


That information, like Apollo’s patient data, is stored in Microsoft Fabric in accordance with the hospital’s data-handling standards.


This continuous learning loop—referred to as “hill-climbing” in AI—means the agent improves with use and contains Apollo’s expanding enterprise knowledge of the review process. This knowledge informs the questions the agent asks clinicians, and its suggested case assessments and recommendations. The clinicians then evaluate the agent’s input and make changes to it before sending the case for review.


“The number of times those questions and recommendations are getting edited is a measurement of the accuracy of the DTH agent,” says Somuveerappan. “If it’s able to recommend the right set of potential questions to ask, and nobody disputes those questions, the agent is picking up knowledge and context.”


As the agent learns to ask clinicians better questions of an incident, frontliners too are gaining knowledge of what information is relevant for an incident review, and for patient safety.


“At the unit level, we’re ready to answer questions from the leadership because the AI has generated questions to help us prepare,” says Juliet Joji Varghese, Apollo’s director of nursing in Chennai. “And we’re also learning from what’s happened at other Apollo hospitals. So, we go beyond looking at why or how something happened, to how we can prevent it in future.”


Juliet Joji Varghese, Apollo Hospital’s director of nursing in Chennai. As the DTH agent learns to ask better questions, frontliners like her are gaining knowledge of what information is relevant for an incident review, and patient safety. Photo by Selvaprakash Lakshmanan for Microsoft.


Another feature of the agent is its ability to spot patterns or trends from the data it collects. This so-called cluster analysis is still a work in progress, says Dr. Sridhar, but the results are promising. One example was cases of patients developing bloodstream infections associated with central lines, which are intravenous lines placed in major veins.


“The agent flagged a cluster of central line-related infections in the bone marrow transplant unit,” she says. “So the unit took action to address that issue.”


### **Impact on patient safety**


In addition to higher case closure rates and a quicker review cycle, Apollo has seen improvements in some safety review criteria since the DTH agent was rolled out.


Based on usage metrics generated by the agent, the number of patient falls and medication errors has dropped over the period July to September this year, compared to the same quarter in 2025.*


Patient safety culture has also improved, observes Dr. Sridhar.


“There has been an almost 30 percent improvement in staff satisfaction in the way that we are handling errors,” she says, citing results of Apollo’s annual safety culture survey this year. In the survey, staff reported higher levels of responsiveness to error, more openness to communication and better reporting on safety incidents compared to 2025. Dr. Sridhar puts this down to the transparency of the review process, enabled by the DTH agent.


“All the data is available to them automatically. They can read the data, draw their conclusions,” she says.


Looking ahead, Dr. Sridhar hopes to apply the same functionalities of the DTH agent to other work processes in Apollo, such as its tumor board review and doctor handovers.


“We hope that using AI-enabled tools will allow us to deliver better care,” she says.


She also wants to use AI to predict what is likely to happen to a patient from the moment they are admitted, and to flag any deviations from their treatment pathways.


“We want to be proactive rather than reactive,” she says. “The best organizations will focus on near-miss events and will be able to identify them before they actually occur. And then re-engineer the process to make sure that it doesn’t happen.”


*Top image caption: Dr. Rohini Sridhar, chief of medical services at Apollo Hospitals. Photo by Selvaprakash Lakshmanan for Microsoft.*


Footnote: Apollo Hospitals tracked patient safety metrics after the DTH agent was deployed. This included data on case closures, falls and medication errors. For case closures, the improvement was calculated by comparing the percentage of agent-prepared cases that were resolved within three days in November 2026 against the case closure rate in December 2025 that was previously tracked by the hospital’s web app. For patient falls and medication errors, the improvement was calculated by comparing the number of such incidents recorded in the quarter from July to September 2026 against the number recorded in the same quarter in 2025.


**Lim Ai Leen reports on AI for Microsoft Source, focusing on how it’s improving lives in Asia. Ai Leen was formerly associate foreign editor at The Straits Times in Singapore and still pens an occasional weekend column. Contact her on[LinkedIn.](https://www.linkedin.com/in/limaileen/)**
